reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Represents the acute suppurative phase of cryptoglandular anal gland infection, of which anal fistula is the chronic sequel
Presents with severe, constant, throbbing perianal pain, a tender fluctuant swelling, erythema, and often fever
Classified by the anatomical space involved: perianal (most common), ischiorectal (ischioanal), intersphincteric, and supralevator
Deep abscesses (intersphincteric or supralevator) may cause severe pain and sepsis with little visible external swelling, requiring examination under anaesthesia and imaging
The mainstay of treatment is prompt incision and drainage; antibiotics alone are inadequate and delay is dangerous
A significant proportion of drained abscesses subsequently develop a fistula-in-ano
Recurrent or atypical abscesses should prompt consideration of Crohn's disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, or malignancy
A spreading, boggy, or crepitant perineum with systemic toxicity suggests necrotising infection (Fournier's gangrene), a surgical emergency
reference.pathophysiology: A perianal abscess usually begins with obstruction and infection of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane (the cryptoglandular mechanism). Pus collects and tracks along planes of least resistance, caudally to the perianal skin, laterally through the external sphincter into the ischioanal fossa, or cephalad above the levators, forming abscesses in the corresponding spaces. It represents the acute phase of the same disease that, once drained or spontaneously discharging, may leave a chronic fistula. Diabetes, immunosuppression, and Crohn's disease predispose to more extensive or recurrent infection.
additionalDifferentials: Fournier's gangrene or other necrotising perineal infection
Anal canal or rectal malignancy presenting with sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia to locate and drain deep collections
MRI of the pelvis for supralevator, complex, or recurrent collections
Endoanal ultrasound to assess deep or intersphincteric collections
Blood glucose and HbA1c, with screening for immunosuppression in recurrent disease
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers if systemic sepsis is suspected
Culture of drained pus and, in atypical cases, biopsy of the abscess wall
redFlags: Spreading erythema, crepitus, or perineal necrosis suggesting Fournier's gangrene
Systemic sepsis, or diabetes or immunosuppression with pain out of proportion to findings
Severe deep pain with minimal external signs suggesting an intersphincteric or supralevator abscess
Recurrent abscesses suggesting Crohn's disease or underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Prompt incision and drainage resolves most simple abscesses, though a notable minority progress to a chronic fistula; delayed treatment or necrotising infection carries substantial morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Relying on antibiotics instead of timely surgical drainage
Missing a deep intersphincteric or supralevator collection because external signs are minimal
Inadequate drainage leaving a loculated cavity and early recurrence
Failing to recognise early Fournier's gangrene in a diabetic or immunosuppressed patient
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Keighley & Williams' Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon
management: Perform prompt incision and drainage as the definitive treatment, as antibiotics alone are inadequate
Undertake examination under anaesthesia to locate and drain deep intersphincteric or supralevator collections
Reserve antibiotics for systemic sepsis, surrounding cellulitis, immunosuppression or diabetes
Provide analgesia, warm baths and wound care with healing by secondary intention
Send drained pus for culture and biopsy the abscess wall in atypical cases
Screen for and optimise diabetes, immunosuppression and Crohn's disease in recurrent or extensive infection
Follow up for fistula-in-ano, which develops in a proportion of drained abscesses
Escalate urgently if necrotising perianal infection is suspected
